title: Choosing your first gun
summary: Hire first, buy later: when your own gun makes sense for Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting, what to try, and how to buy a used gun safely and legally.

body.html: A common beginner mistake is to buy a gun before knowing what suits you. A gun has to fit you: your height, the width of your shoulders, your face and your master eye. So the first step is not a shop but a shooting ground and a coach.

For the first months the ground's hire gun is enough for many beginners. Hire guns often come with a first lesson, cartridges, glasses and ear protection. You learn safety and technique, try different models and find out whether you enjoy Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting.
A competition rule matters here: two shooters in the same squad may not use the same gun. If you hire a gun for a competition, make sure nobody else in your squad shoots with it.

It is time to think about your own gun when you train regularly, know which discipline you will shoot and your coach has seen how you mount the gun. Your own gun, fitted to you, helps you shoot more consistently, because it comes up the same way each time.

Check the rules before you buy. In both disciplines the gun must be a smooth-bore shotgun, no larger than 12 gauge, with barrels at least 66 cm (26 in) long. A semi-automatic is allowed, a pump-action is not, so even a cheap pump gun is no good here (see Types of shotgun).

Try before you buy. Good shops and grounds let you shoot demonstration guns. Compare an over-and-under with a semi-automatic, 28 with 30 inch barrels, and different weights. Look less at the engraving and more at how the gun comes to the shoulder and moves with the target.

For many adult beginners a good start is a 12-gauge competition over-and-under with interchangeable chokes and 30 inch barrels. Juniors and smaller shooters may be better off with a lighter model or a 20 gauge. A left-handed shooter needs a stock bent slightly to the left (cast on), so that the left eye lines up over the rib.
New or used? A new gun has a warranty and a known history. A used one can cost noticeably less, and a quality gun that has been looked after lasts for decades. But buying a used gun blind is risky.

Before you buy a used gun, show it to a gunsmith. They check the barrels for dents, bulges and rust inside, and whether the gun closes tightly with no wobble between the barrels and the action. They also check the triggers and ejectors, the chokes and the stock. In many countries guns are tested at an official proof house and stamped with proof marks; the gunsmith can tell you whether the marks are in order.

Buy only through legal channels: from a licensed dealer, or with the change of owner registered as your country's law requires. Almost everywhere you need a licence for a shotgun, and the laws differ. A gun without papers or of unknown origin is not a saving but a serious problem.

Budget for more than the gun: glasses and hearing protection, a slip or hard case, a cleaning kit, spare chokes, a safe and perhaps a stock fitting. Above all, budget for cartridges and lessons: a few lessons often help your scores more than a more expensive gun.

key_points.html: Start with the ground's hire gun and a coach; try several models before you buy.
Buy your own once you train regularly and have had a fitting.
Two shooters in the same squad may not share one gun in competition.
Have a used gun checked by a gunsmith.
Buy only through legal channels; licences depend on the country.

did_you_know.html: A good over-and-under that is properly cared for can serve several generations of shooters. That is why a quality used gun is a common first choice.

quiz.q: What is a sensible way to start choosing a first gun?

options.text: Buy the most expensive model you can find
Shoot hire guns and try several with a coach
Order one online from the photos
Buy the same model as a champion

quiz.explain: A gun has to fit you, and you only find out after shooting several models.

quiz.q: May two shooters of the same squad use one gun in competition?

options.text: Yes, if it is a hire gun

quiz.explain: The rules of both disciplines forbid sharing one gun within a squad or group.

quiz.q: When is it time for a beginner to buy their own gun?

options.text: Before the very first lesson at a ground
Right after the first few shots
As soon as a shop has a sale
When you train regularly and have had a fitting

quiz.explain: Experience and a fitting first; then the gun will suit you.
